stances.claim: The SC has struggled with heavy caseload since long before CJ joined in 1995 -- as early as Francisco v. Permskul (May 12, 1989) the Court already noted 'the tremendous number of cases' filed amid restored democracy -- and the problem has worsened: Gio-Samar v. DOTC (March 12, 2019, unanimous) admitted a 'staggering' 14,491 cases as of December 31, 2016, with each of the 15 justices carrying an average of 966 cases ('a gargantuan load too heavy to shoulder').
stances.rhetorical_move: long-arc problem statement with empirical evidence

stances.claim: Justice Jardeleza's US learning visit produced a report whose tracking -- minute and unsigned resolutions, routing of NLRC/SEC quasi-judicial decisions and capital-penalty reviews to the CA -- recovered earlier PH solutions, but did not track CJ-specific reforms; nonetheless, Jardeleza specifically cited CJ Panganiban's Jan. 26, 2006 Committee on Zero Backlog (included as Annex A) and the 'judicial bayanihan' practice where old cases were surrendered to a pool from which lighter-caseload justices voluntarily plucked them.
stances.rhetorical_move: Jardeleza-report relay with self-citation of CJ reforms

stances.claim: Post-CJ-retirement, the bayanihan practice was abandoned 'for reasons unknown to me,' and the July 31, 2007 SC approval of Committee recommendations (500-cases-for-signed-decisions in next 6.5 years; 1,000-output-until-cleared; thereafter 500-1,000/year for signed decisions, rest by minute resolutions) was not implemented -- caseload grew steadily.
stances.rhetorical_move: implementation-failure observation with self-disclosure of ignorance

stances.claim: Jardeleza's smart-technology recommendation -- differentiating original-jurisdiction from appellate-jurisdiction cases, tracking (a) denied-outright / (b) ordered-to-file-comment / (c) given-due-course-with-strict-deadlines cases, and shortening filing periods (Comments to 10 days Division / 20 days En Banc, no extensions, no 'Replies' except 'in extremely meritorious cases'; Memoranda 20 days no extensions) -- provides the modern docket-management infrastructure CJ Panganiban's plan lacked.

CJ Peralta's 'Ten-Point Program' -- with 'Elimination of backlog in the Supreme Court and all other courts' as the first item -- combined with faithful implementation of both the Committee on Zero Backlog report and Jardeleza's recommendations, will 'finally solve the perennial problem of justice delayed is justice denied.' Peralta's signature method of giving reforms 'transparency and permanency by integrating them in the Rules of Court' will make progress trackable.

notable_anecdotes: The 966-cases-per-justice arithmetic -- 14,491 cases divided by 15 justices -- making the 'staggering' Gio-Samar admission into a per-justice burden the reader can intuit.

The Jardeleza-as-emissary detail -- the SC sent the Gio-Samar writer himself on a US learning visit to study how Scotus decides all cases within one year -- and 'Recently, J Jardeleza (now retired) sent me a copy of his report,' converting CJ from observer to recipient of the institutional document.

The Annex A self-citation -- CJ Panganiban's Jan. 26, 2006 Committee on Zero Backlog resolution preserved as exhibit material in Jardeleza's report -- establishing the prior reform's documentary durability.

The 'judicial bayanihan' practice -- old cases surrendered to a pool from which 'justices with light caseloads voluntarily plucked and decided them' -- using a quintessentially Filipino communal-labor concept (bayanihan) for SC docket-clearing, a culturally-resonant institutional innovation.
The 'for reasons unknown to me' admission of bayanihan's post-retirement abandonment -- CJ's rare self-disclosure of ignorance, acknowledging institutional discontinuity he cannot explain.

The July 31, 2007 Committee numbers -- 500 signed-decisions / 6.5 years, 1,000 maintenance output, 500-1,000 thereafter -- preserved verbatim from the Court resolution to make the implementation gap audit-able.

The Jardeleza operational specifics -- 10 days for Division Comments, 20 days for En Banc, no extensions, no 'Replies' except 'in extremely meritorious cases,' 20 days for Memoranda -- making the docket-management reform concrete rather than aspirational.

The 'transparency and permanency' attribution to CJ Peralta's signature integration-in-Rules-of-Court method -- a procedural-architecture endorsement that explains why this attempt may succeed where 2007 didn't.

The Zoom webinar postscript with full meeting ID and passcode -- Aug. 24, 2-4 p.m., on PH Foreign Investment Rules / Asean Comprehensive Investment Agreement -- converting the column's tail into a civic-event invitation.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban traces the long-standing SC caseload problem from Francisco v. Permskul (May 12, 1989) -- where the Court already noted 'the tremendous number of cases' filed in restored-democracy PH -- to Gio-Samar v. DOTC (March 12, 2019), where the unanimous Court candidly admitted a 'staggering' 14,491 cases on its docket as of December 31, 2016. With 15 justices, that meant an average of 966 cases each, 'clearly a gargantuan load too heavy to shoulder.' Knowing the Supreme Court of the United States has no backlog and decides all its cases within one year, the Court sent the Gio-Samar writer Justice Francis H. Jardeleza on a US learning visit; Jardeleza (now retired) recently sent CJ his report. The report tracked earlier PH solutions -- minute and unsigned resolutions, routing of NLRC/SEC quasi-judicial decisions and capital-penalty reviews to the Court of Appeals -- but did not track CJ-specific reforms, though it specifically cited the Committee on Zero Backlog CJ Panganiban created on January 26, 2006 (included as Annex A). While awaiting the Committee's report, the Court practiced a judicial 'bayanihan' whereby old cases were surrendered to a pool from which justices with light caseloads voluntarily plucked and decided them; 'After I left, the Court, for reasons unknown to me, abandoned the practice.' On July 31, 2007 (after CJ retired), the Court approved the Committee's recommendations: '(1) ...accept only 500 cases for signed decisions in the next 6.5 years... and (2) ...maintain its output of 1,000 signed decisions until the backlog is cleared. The Court may thereafter decide to accept anywhere from 500 to 1,000 cases per year for signed decisions,' with the rest decided by minute resolutions. Obviously, this was not implemented -- the caseload grew. Jardeleza's report recommends a better method of case selection and docket management via smart technology, including differentiating and tracking separately (1) original-jurisdiction vs appellate-jurisdiction cases and (2) cases (a) denied outright, (b) ordered to file comment, and (c) given due course for full signed decision with strict deadlines. He also suggests shortening filing periods: 'Comments' to 10 days for Division cases and 20 days for En Banc, without extensions and without requiring 'Replies' except in 'extremely meritorious cases,' and 20 days for 'Memoranda' also without extensions. CJ Diosdado M. Peralta began his term with a 'Ten-Point Program,' the first item being the 'Elimination of backlog in the Supreme Court and all other courts' (CJ's January 12, 2020 column). Together with faithful implementation of both the Committee on Zero Backlog and Jardeleza's recommendations, the Court will 'finally solve the perennial problem of justice delayed is justice denied.' CJ Peralta is noted for giving reforms 'transparency and permanency by integrating them in the Rules of Court,' making progress trackable. The column closes with a postscript: an August 24 Zoom roundtable on 'Philippine Foreign Investment Rules' as related to the Asean Comprehensive Investment Agreement, organized by the Asean Law Institute, the Asean Law Association (Philippine Chapter), and the Asian Institute of Management.
